description: We’re a team of curious problem-solvers brought together by a shared interest in space, science, and technology. Combining skills in software development, AI, data analysis, and design, we aim to turn complex scientific ideas into practical, interactive solutions. Through the NASA Space Apps Challenge, we’re excited to explore bold ideas, learn from one another, and build something that makes space exploration more accessible and understandable.
summary:
Marswalk is a mission tool for one crewed walk at Jezero Crater on Mars. Mars maps today are made for whole regions, but an astronaut on foot needs the next 300 metres. We built two tools on NASA data: a Roblox simulator to rehearse the walk, and a wrist navigator to carry it out.

Our goal is to find rock that formed in water, where signs of ancient life could have survived. We layered seven kinds of data from four NASA missions on a 10 m grid: HiRISE images and elevation, THEMIS, CRISM, Curiosity RAD, Perseverance MEDA and the rover’s path. Every value is labelled measured, modeled or simulated.

Each square gets a science score and a hazard score. Slopes above 20 degrees and squares with no data are no-go. Each site must pass five checks. Then the navigator finds the cheapest safe road and ranks sites for science, safety, time and distance, with spacesuit speed and oxygen built in.

On the walk it shows bearing, distance and the hazard on the next 300 m. It warns about solar storms and routes the astronaut to shelter, analyses unknown objects, and flags ground no rover has visited. The simulator rebuilds 2 by 2 km of real Jezero terrain with three scored missions.

Checked against Perseverance’s real drive, 98.7% rates safe and none is no-go. Limits: weather and object readings are simulated, and the planned ESP32 wrist unit was not built, so the navigator is a web prototype. We used Claude (Anthropic) to help generate the navigator code, data scripts and slides.
details:
The problem

When astronauts land on Mars, they will leave the habitat on foot to do science. Each walk is small. It covers a few kilometres at most, and the decisions that keep the crew alive are about the ground right in front of them. Mars maps today are not made for this. Tools like NASA’s Mars Trek are built to look at whole regions or the whole planet. They cannot tell an astronaut which slope is too steep for a spacesuit, where the sand is loose, how much oxygen the trip will cost, or where to hide when a solar storm arrives. The challenge asked for a map, tool or interface for exactly this job. Our answer is Marswalk.

Our idea

Marswalk follows one walk through three stages: plan it, rehearse it, carry it out. We built two tools for this, and both are built on NASA data of the same place. The first is a Roblox simulator where a crew can practise the walk on real Jezero terrain before they go. The second is a wrist navigator, a small screen worn on the suit that guides the astronaut during the walk. Because both tools show the same real terrain, what the crew learns in the rehearsal carries over to the walk.

Science goal and location

Our science goal is to find rock that formed in water, because that is where signs of ancient life could have survived. We chose Jezero Crater for two reasons. First, it once held a lake, and a river built a delta on its western side. The delta is one of the best places on Mars to look for water-formed rock. Second, the Perseverance rover has been driving there since 2021. That gave us something rare: a real drive on the real ground that we could compare with our map. Our habitat sits at Perseverance’s landing site, and the navigator covers 13 by 11 kilometres around it.

The data

The brief asked for at least three kinds of data. We layered seven kinds from four NASA missions on one grid of 10 metre squares, about 1.4 million squares in total.

  • Optical: the HiRISE image mosaic from Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter is our base map.
  • Topographic: the HiRISE elevation model gives slope, roughness, sunlight and radio line of sight to the habitat.
  • Thermal: THEMIS thermal inertia from Mars Odyssey shows loose sand and cold ground.
  • Spectral: six CRISM scenes show where water-altered minerals are.
  • Radiation: Curiosity’s RAD instrument measured the dose on the surface at Gale Crater. We use it as the base of our radiation model.
  • Atmospheric: weather measurements from Perseverance’s MEDA station guided our weather model.
  • Ground truth: Perseverance’s driven path shows where a rover has already been.

The layers have very different detail. The images show 25 centimetres, but the thermal data only shows 100 metres. Not all of the data is equally certain either, and we say so. Every value in both tools is labelled as measured, modeled or simulated.

How it picks a safe path

Our algorithm works in four steps.

First, every square gets its facts from the data layers. If a square has no data, it is no-go. We do not guess.

Second, every square gets two scores. The science score combines minerals, variety of ground, and how unexplored the square is. The hazard score combines slope, rocks, sand, roughness, cold, radiation, elevation, sunlight and radio link. Slope counts the most, then rocks and sand. The hazard formula is 0.6 times the weighted average plus 0.4 times the worst factor. We added the worst factor on purpose. With a simple average, one deadly problem can hide behind many safe numbers. Any slope above 20 degrees is no-go for a crew on foot.

Third, each candidate site must pass five yes or no checks. Is it worth the trip? Can we reach it? Can we get there and back in time? Is the route safe on average? Is there no single dangerous spot on the way?

Fourth, the navigator finds the cheapest safe road with Dijkstra’s algorithm. Each step costs more when the ground is more hazardous, so the route bends around danger instead of crossing it. Then the sites are ranked out of 100 points: 40 for science, 30 for safety, 15 for time and 15 for distance.

Spacesuit mobility is built in. An astronaut walks at 2.9 km/h on flat ground and slows down on climbs. The trip must fit inside the oxygen supply with a 25% reserve. The result is strict. Out of 24 candidate sites, only 4 pass all five checks on foot. With a crewed rover, 21 pass.

The wrist navigator

The navigator is what the astronaut uses outside. Before the walk, it shows the ranked sites. The 24 sites are of six kinds, such as water minerals, layered outcrops and unexplored ground, and the crew can add their own. Choosing a site opens a briefing page with a real close-up image, an elevation map, the height profile of the route and the result of the five checks.

During the walk, the main screen shows the route on the real image, with bearing, distance, time to go and the hazard on the next 300 metres. The status bar shows oxygen, radiation dose, outside temperature and the link to the habitat. The navigator has three modes: on foot, crewed rover and robot rover. Everything is designed to be read at a glance through a helmet, with large numbers and a fixed colour code.

The navigator also watches for danger. If a solar particle event starts, the radiation dose rises fast, so the navigator finds the nearest shelter and re-routes the astronaut there. It also warns about dust devils, dust storms, strong wind, cold and a lost radio link.

Two more features help with science and trust. The object analyser scans unknown objects on the route and gives one clear instruction: bring back, do not touch, keep clear, or leave in place. And the navigator admits doubt. It warns the astronaut when the route crosses ground that no rover has visited, or where the data is coarse.

We planned to run this on an ESP32 wrist unit. We ran out of time, so the navigator is a web prototype with the same layout and screens.

The Roblox simulator

The simulator is where the crew rehearses. It rebuilds about 2 by 2 kilometres of Jezero, including the crater floor and the western delta, from the HiRISE elevation model. The player walks it in first person. The helmet view shows location, a compass to the next waypoint, oxygen, battery, radiation and temperature. Oxygen runs out in about an hour, so the player has to plan the way back to the habitat.

A tablet called the Mars Navigator shows five data layers: optical, topography, radiation, geophysical and thermal. The player can plan a route with four strategies: fastest, safest, balanced or shortest. Each route gets a risk score from 0 to 100, and slopes that are too steep are avoided. The player can also scan objects, collect samples and log discoveries. There are three missions: exploring the delta, a hazardous expedition, and a scientific investigation. Each one ends with a debrief that scores safety, science and efficiency. Every reading in the game carries a label: measured, modeled, interpreted, simulated or fictional.

How we checked it

A hazard map is only useful if it matches the real ground. So we took the path that Perseverance really drove and scored it with our map. 98.7% of the drive rates as safe, and none of it is no-go. We want to be clear about one thing: we tuned one sand threshold using this drive, so this is a consistency check and not an independent test.

Limits

We tried not to pretend. The weather events are a model and not live data. Radiation is modeled from Gale Crater, not measured at Jezero. The object readings in the analyser are simulated. The dose limit and the shelter rules are our own assumptions. In the simulator there is no day and night cycle, the radio link indicator is a demo, and the rover mission was designed but not built.

Tools

We used Roblox Studio with Luau for the simulator, HTML, CSS and JavaScript for the navigator, and Python for processing the NASA data. We used Claude, an AI model from Anthropic, to help generate the navigator code, the data scripts and our slides, following our own algorithm design.

Why it matters

A Marswalk is the moment when all the planning meets the real ground. Marswalk turns orbital data into answers an astronaut can use: where to go, which way is safe, how long it takes, and when to turn back. The method is not tied to Jezero. It can be run for any site that has the same kinds of data. Our next steps are to build the ESP32 wrist unit, add the rover mission to the simulator, and replace the weather model with measured MEDA data.
